question: Climate science looks into temperature changes, sea level rise, and the occurrence of extreme weather events but it does not study the stability and response of our civilisation to climate and ecological shocks. Climate change could cause significant disruptions to ecosystems, society, and economies, potentially making large areas of the Earth uninhabitable.

As civilisation cannot exist in uninhabitable places, climate change may cause civilisation collapse to a greater or lesser extent. The latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Synthesis Report1 clearly states that there is a rapidly closing window of opportunity to secure a liveable and sustainable future for all.

The UN Emissions Gap Report 20232 states that the current trend would lead us to a temperature rise of nearly three degrees Celsius this century, which could make the world pass several tipping points. 1.
What is the Commission doing to ensure that civilisation survives the climate and ecological shocks that are the result of climate change and biodiversity loss?
Is the Commission adequately preparing emergency plans for abrupt societal and natural crises caused by climate change?
Will the Commission ensure that sufficient resources are given to scientific studies that explore how resilient our civilisation will be to climate and ecological shocks?

Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Synthesis Report: Climate Change 2023: https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_SYR_LongerReport.pdf. UN Emissions Gap Report 2023: https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/43922/EGR2023.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.4.2024) The EU sets ambitious climate and biodiversity policies, consistent with the goals of the Paris Agreement (PA) and the Kunming Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF).

It is based on science and informed by the reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)1 and of the Intergovernmental Science and Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES)2. The EU is committed to climate neutrality and resilience by 2050, as enshrined in the European Climate Law3, along with an interim target of 55% net greenhouse gas emission reduction by 2030.

The Commission adopted a Communication on the 2040 climate target4, while the EU Biodiversity Strategy5 and EU Adaptation Strategy6 sets out how the EU can set nature on a path to recovery and become climate resilient by 2050. In recent years, Europe has faced the devastating impacts of large wildfires, exacerbated by climate change.

To enhance its preparedness for future wildfires, the EU is scaling up the rescEU firefighting fleet78 The Horizon Europe Framework programme for Research and Innovation9 dedicates 35% of its budget to climate-related objectives. EU-funded projects deliver policy-relevant outcomes that underpin IPCC and IPBES assessments and inform the implementation of the European Green Deal and of the PA and GBF.

Some of the most pertinent initiatives addressing societal resilience to climate change are the ongoing EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change10, the activities under Horizon Europe Cluster 3 on Civil Security for Society11 and Cluster 5 on Climate, Energy and Mobility12.
Other Union programmes such as LIFE13 have invested in research and demonstration projects on nature-based solutions14 delivering multiple benefits for climate, nature and people.

response operations and aims at maintaining this increased capacity for the 2024 wildfire season. The number of wildfire response capacities is expected to considerably increase as of 2026. 8 As of 2026, 14 airplanes and up to 9 helicopters will be procured under the rescEU’s permanent fleet. These helicopters can also be deployed for addressing other climate change-induced disasters, such as extreme floods.
